Summary

Where Things Stand

NEAR is a sharded proof-of-stake layer-1 whose investment case has migrated from ‘high-throughput smart-contract chain’ to ‘cross-chain settlement and value-capture layer.’ As of 11 November 2026, NEAR trades at $3.72 with a $4.88 billion market capitalization (rank #24), 82.4% below its January 2022 all-time high of $20.40 and up 41.3% year-over-year. The engine of the long-term thesis is NEAR Intents, a chain-abstraction and solver network that has settled $37.3 billion all-time (88% of it in the trailing twelve months) and now averages $125 million per day. Since the fee switch went live, the protocol has captured $11.63 million of cumulative net revenue against $60.97 million of gross Intents fees, with the monthly capture rate rising from roughly 11% early in 2026 to 39.2% in October. Net revenue currently offsets 17.8% of token emissions.

The thesis, stated so it can be tested:

  1. Cross-chain volume keeps compounding through Intents.
  2. The protocol converts a rising share of that volume into net revenue that is routed to buybacks — the buyback wallet has accumulated 2.25 million NEAR (about $8.1 million) with zero outflows observed in the latest on-chain window.
  3. Governance tightens supply, with the House of Stake approving a cut of maximum inflation from 2.5% to 1.6% on 2 November 2026 (HSP-029, phased over 24 months), which shrinks the volume threshold V* at which net issuance flips negative to roughly 2.6 times the current run-rate.

Verdict

At $4.88 billion, NEAR trades at about 163 times annualized captured revenue and 68.3 times annualized gross fees. For today’s price to be justified at a mature 60 times net revenue, captured revenue must grow roughly 2.7 times to $81 million per year — almost exactly the growth the deflation model requires. The market has already paid for delivery of the disclosed plan; upside therefore requires outperformance against that plan, not closure of a mispricing. Every load-bearing number in this report is re-runnable from public endpoints without API keys; sources that cannot be re-run (Nansen research, ETF flow tallies) are marked ‘cited, not re-runnable’ and never support a main claim alone.

Chapter 2

Research Design and Data Infrastructure

The thesis, stated falsifiably

A long-term thesis earns the name only if specific observations can kill it. This report expresses the NEAR case as three claims, each mapped to a measurable quantity and each carrying an explicit falsifier in Chapter 6. Claim A (demand): cross-chain swap volume routed and settled through NEAR Intents continues to compound, because the product competes on cross-chain user experience and solver economics rather than on L1 throughput. Claim B (capture): the protocol retains a rising share of the fees generated by that volume — through the owned front-end, quote improvement, and business-to-business integrations — and routes the proceeds to buybacks held in an on-chain wallet whose flows anyone can audit. Claim C (scarcity): token supply policy tightens on the committed schedule, so the mint shrinks while the revenue sink grows, putting a deflationary crossover V* within sight at plausible volume multiples. None of these claims depends on narratives about AI agents, confidential computing, or tokenized equities. Those initiatives are real and are covered by third-party research, but they are treated here as optionality, not as load-bearing assumptions. If Claims A through C hold, the investment case stands on its own; if any one fails at the thresholds defined in Chapter 6, the thesis is wrong regardless of how compelling the narrative becomes.

The evidence standard

Two tiers of evidence are used, and the distinction is enforced throughout. Tier 1 is re-runnable without API keys: CoinPaprika for price and market capitalization, Binance's public data mirror for candle history, DefiLlama for Intents volume and fees, the NEAR mainnet RPC for staking and protocol parameters, NearBlocks for daily activity and wallet flows, revenue.near.org for the on-chain revenue dashboard, and the BigQuery public dataset for full on-chain history. Every number that supports a main claim is Tier 1, carries its endpoint in Appendix A, and was retrieved on 11 November 2026 (08:36-09:00 UTC). Tier 2 is cited, not re-runnable: Nansen research (API-key gated), ETF flow tallies (no free API), and press coverage of governance events. Tier 2 adds color and cross-checks; it never carries a claim by itself.

What ‘priced for delivery’ means

Verdict language matters. A ‘valuation gap’ argument claims the market is wrong about current fundamentals, so price should converge to fair value with high probability. A ‘priced for delivery’ argument claims the market has fairly priced a continuation of disclosed trends, so future returns require outperformance relative to those trends, and the downside is defined by the falsifiers rather than by the market's error. This report adopts the second framing on purpose: Chapter 5 quantifies the growth already embedded in the market capitalization, and Chapter 6 defines the observations that would flip the verdict. The report deliberately does not argue a valuation gap, and the conclusion should be read as a statement about expectations, not about mispricing.

Chapter 3

Network Fundamentals and Onchain Evidence

Market structure

NEAR closed at $3.72 on 11 November 2026 with a $4.88 billion market capitalization and $474 million of 24-hour turnover. The asset remains a deep-drawdown position: 82.4% below the January 2022 all-time high of $20.40, even after a 41.3% gain over the past year. The Binance candle history shows the same picture with more texture — a +42.6% 365-day return, price below the 50-day moving average ($4.64) but above the 200-day ($2.65), and 97% annualized 30-day realized volatility. In plain terms: a corrective phase inside a one-year uptrend, with event-driven bursts around the fee switch (October 2025), the buyback wallet going live (March 2026), the Bitwise NRR ETF launch (29 September 2026), and the HSP-029 inflation vote (2 November 2026). Figure 1 marks these on the price series. Supply is 1,311.4 million NEAR total with 1,249.8 million circulating per NearBlocks — the vesting overhang that dominates younger tokens is absent here.

The Intents engine: demand evidence

NEAR Intents routes user intents to competing solvers across 30+ chains and settles them on NEAR. The demand data is the strongest part of the bull case. All-time volume is $37.3 billion across 701 days of history, of which $32.9 billion — 88% — settled in the trailing twelve months; the trailing-365-day total is 7.5 times the prior-year total, and the 90-day average of $134 million per day is 3.3 times the year-ago 90-day average. The 30-day run-rate is $125 million per day, with a peak month of $4.80 billion in September 2026, $3.99 billion in October, and $131 million per day over the first ten days of November. By 30-day volume, NEAR Intents ranks nineteenth among 1,617 venues tracked by DefiLlama — in the same band as major aggregators and DEXs. The revenue dashboard reports 659 thousand unique users expressing intents in the past 30 days and $142.6 million of confidential TVL. Fee capture is newer than volume and is scaling fast. Gross Intents fees are $59.8 million all-time ($5.46 million over the last 30 days; $6.39 million in October), which the dashboard independently corroborates at $60.97 million. Net protocol revenue — the share retained after payouts to solvers, partners, and dApps — has compounded from $27.6 thousand in August 2025 to $2.50 million in October 2026, $11.63 million cumulative. October's capture rate was 39.2% of gross fees, versus 19.5% lifetime, and the dashboard's mechanism split (front-end 20.1%, B2B partners 10.2%, quote improvement 3.6% over 30 days) shows the capture is diversified across three levers rather than one. Nansen's independent accounting put lifetime capture at 16.4% and trailing-30-day capture at 28.4% as of 6 October — a different window and definition, but the same direction. Figures 2 and 3 show the volume build-up and the fee-to-revenue conversion.

The counter-evidence: L1 activity has contracted sharply

An evidence-first report must lead with the weakest link, and here it is the NEAR layer-1 itself. Daily transactions averaged 4.26 million over 1-10 November 2025; over the same window in 2026 they averaged 706 thousand — an 83% decline. Daily active accounts fell 67%, from 249 thousand to 81 thousand. The December 2024 peak of 8.25 million transactions per day is far behind. Layer-1 fees are immaterial at $4.6 thousand per day ($1.66 million annualized), so the base chain's own fee market cannot fund anything. The honest reading: the 2024-25 transaction boom was driven by short-lived gaming and social applications; that activity ended, and NEAR's economic center of gravity moved to the Intents layer, which settles cross-chain value that mostly does not originate as NEAR L1 transactions. This matters for the thesis in two ways. First, the classic 'broad on-chain usage' argument for NEAR has already failed — that falsifier has fired, and what remains is a narrower and cleaner value-capture story. Second, the fee base is now one product wide: thirteen months of fee history, concentrated in Intents, with the owned front-end routing roughly a quarter of Q3 volume by third-party accounting. That concentration cuts both ways — it makes capture efficient (the front-end captures 100% of its fees) and it makes the revenue engine fragile if product mix or routing behavior shifts. Figure 4 shows the L1 contraction that any NEAR thesis must now absorb.

TVL and stablecoins: a shrinking DeFi footprint

NEAR is not a DeFi destination chain, and the data says so plainly. Chain TVL is $174 million, down 11% year-over-year; stablecoin circulating on NEAR is $131 million, down 21%, and now equals 76% of all TVL. For scale: NEAR settles more Intents volume every 36 hours than the entire value locked in its DeFi ecosystem. This is consistent with the clearing-house view of NEAR — value passes through and is monetized as fees rather than parked as TVL — but it removes another classic leg of L1 theses (the 'TVL follows activity' multiplier). Any bull case that leans on DeFi growth on NEAR L1 is contradicted by the current data; the bull case that survives leans on volume, capture, and supply policy. Figure 5 shows the flat-to-down trajectory.

Staking and the validator set

The chain itself is stable and well-secured. The RPC reports 351 active validators with 582.1 million NEAR staked — 44.4% of total supply — at protocol version 88, with 43,200-block epochs (about 7 hours at the current 0.577-second average block time) and a cumulative 5.48 billion transactions since genesis. At the on-chain maximum inflation of 2.5% with 90% of new issuance flowing to stakers, the gross staking yield is 5.07%; an independent survey in October put it at 4.90% using a 45.9% staking ratio, which confirms the formula. The open question is behavioral: when the inflation cut takes effect and gross yield falls toward 3.2%, does the staking ratio hold? A large unstaking wave would raise effective float; a stable ratio would confirm that stakers price the cut as dilution relief rather than yield loss. This is tracked as part of falsifier F3 in Chapter 6.

Chapter 4

Tokenomics and the Deflationary Mechanics

Supply and the inflation path

Total supply is 1,311.4 million NEAR with no material unlock overhang, so supply dynamics are governed by issuance policy and fee sinks, not vesting cliffs. Today the protocol mints at a maximum rate of 2.5% per year — the RPC protocol configuration reports max_inflation_rate = 1/40 at protocol version 88 equal to 89,822 NEAR per day by formula; the revenue dashboard’s on-chain accounting counts 87,604 NEAR per day actually emitted. Per the passed-but-not-yet-live governance proposal HSP-029, the House of Stake voted on 2 November 2026 to reduce the maximum to 1.6%, phased in over 24 months, with roughly 90% of issuance to stakers and 10% to the treasury — about 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided in the first two years and daily issuance falling from roughly 89.5 thousand to 57.3 thousand NEAR at full implementation. Two precision points matter for an evidence-based thesis: the RPC still reports 2.5% as of 11 November 2026, so the cut is a committed expectation rather than a present on-chain fact; and the proposal’s issuance numbers match our own RPC-derived arithmetic, which is exactly the kind of cross-check this report requires.

Where the fees go: capture plumbing and the buyback wallet

All Intents fees are denominated in NEAR. Gross fees are split among solvers, integrators, and the protocol; the retained net revenue flows to three auditable on-chain wallets. The dashboard’s all-time breakdown: fefundsadmin.sputnik-dao.near (front-end fees; 2.00 million NEAR, 46.5%), buybacks.multisignature.near (1.74 million NEAR, 40.5%), and 1csfundsadmin.sputnik-dao.near (B2B; 0.56 million NEAR, 12.9%). The buyback wallet was created on 18 March 2026 (its first on-chain transaction), has since received 1.74 million NEAR of revenue, and holds a balance of 2,245,764 NEAR — about $8.1 million — verified directly against the RPC. Flow history from NearBlocks shows the sink behaving as designed: over 31 October to 11 November the wallet received 107,266 NEAR from intents.near and sent out exactly zero; across a March-May audit window the only outflows were 25 NEAR of operational dust across two transactions.

Scaled against issuance, revenue currently removes 17.8% of what the mint creates — up from 0.2% in August 2025 and a peak of 25.2% in September 2026. An independent sanity check from the CEO of SVRN, the Nasdaq-listed NEAR treasury company, described the network as ‘issuing more than six times as much new NEAR as those buybacks removed’ with about $1.9 million of buybacks in the trailing 30 days as of early October — directionally identical to our 17-25% offset range. Figure 6 shows the monthly offset ratio; the trend is up, but the level remains a fraction of the mint.

The deflation threshold V*

V* is the daily Intents volume at which the revenue sink equals the mint, so net issuance flips negative. With take rate τ (net revenue divided by volume), price P, supply S, and inflation i: V* = (i × S / 365 × P) / τ. October’s effective take was 6.28 basis points ($2.502 million net revenue on $3.99 billion volume). At the current 2.5% inflation, V* is $516 million per day — 4.1 times the current $125 million. At the 1.6% target, V* falls to $330 million per day — 2.6 times current. Two sensitivities are worth internalizing. Each additional basis point of take rate cuts V* by about 14%, so capture improvements and volume growth compound toward the crossover. And the crossover requires the sink to keep behaving like a sink: bought-back NEAR is held in the multisig today, not burned, so the mechanism is only as deflationary as the wallet’s custody discipline — which is why wallet outflows are falsifier F4. Figure 7 plots the model; every input is re-computable from Appendix A and Appendix B.

The inflation cut is not a free lunch for stakers, and the report should not pretend otherwise: gross staking yield falls from about 5.1% to about 3.2% as the cut phases in. For a staker, the exchange is roughly neutral in NEAR terms (yield falls in proportion to dilution) and mildly positive in float terms; for a non-staker it is unambiguously positive, since the dilution they absorb without staking drops by about 36%. A new, small demand sink is also worth noting: staking NEAR to pay for confidential AI inference had attracted more than 750 thousand NEAR by Q3 2026 — a non-DeFi yield consumer that did not exist a year ago (cited, not re-runnable).

Chapter 5

Valuation Framework and Reproducible Models

Fee multiples versus peers

The uniform, re-runnable comparison is price-to-sales on gross fees: market capitalization divided by annualized 30-day fees, using DefiLlama dailyFees for every chain and CoinPaprika for every market cap, retrieved the same day. On that metric NEAR trades at 68.3 times annualized gross Intents fees ($71.5 million run-rate) — the cheapest among the majors in the comparison set, against a peer median of 434 times: Tron 100x, Arbitrum 164x, Solana 234x, BNB Chain 624x, Avalanche 888x, Ethereum 1,028x. Measured on captured revenue — the $30.0 million October net run-rate — NEAR’s multiple is 163 times, because only a fraction of gross fees is retained. Table 3 and Figure 8 lay out the comparison. Three caveats keep this honest: peer fee definitions vary (some exclude tips and MEV); NEAR’s fee base is thirteen months old and one product wide; and cheapness on a young fee base prices growth risk, not stability. The multiple gap versus peers is real, but it is a statement about capture uncertainty and product concentration — not about a mispriced asset.

What the market is pricing: the implied-growth model

Flip the multiple around and the valuation question becomes concrete: how much revenue growth is embedded in $4.88 billion? Hold a mature-multiple assumption of 60 times net revenue — between Tron’s 100 times on mature fees and a discount for NEAR’s concentration — and the market is paying for a net revenue run-rate of $81.4 million per year, which is 2.7 times the current $30.0 million. At the current 163 times multiple, the same growth implies a $13.3 billion network (+172%); but expecting a 163 times multiple to persist through maturity is historically aggressive. Table 4 runs the scenario grid: volume multiple times take rate into net revenue, then priced at both multiples. The bull row is the instructive one — at 2.75 times current volume ($344 million per day, essentially the post-cut V* level), net revenue reaches $79 million and the mature-multiple value equals today’s price almost exactly. The bull case, in other words, is already in the price. These are model outputs, not price targets; the model file ships with this report and every input is in Appendix B.

Does volume lead price? A lead-lag test

If the market trades NEAR on Intents fundamentals, volume should lead or at least move with price. It does not. Cross-correlating daily NEAR returns (Binance) with daily Intents volume growth (DefiLlama) across lags of −14 to +14 days over 527 days since June 2025 yields r = +0.01 at lag zero, with a maximum absolute correlation of just 0.07 at −14 days — statistically indistinguishable from noise. Figure 9 shows the correlogram. The interpretation cuts both ways. Bullish: volume growth is not yet priced tick-by-tick, so fundamental delivery can still surprise. Bearish: price is not tethered to the fundamental series, so delivery alone may not lift the price — the connection runs through regime shifts like the ETF launch and governance votes (visible in Figure 1’s event windows) rather than through daily flow data. For an evidence-based holder the practical conclusion is that the falsifier dashboard, not the price chart, is the tracking instrument.

Verdict

On re-runnable evidence, NEAR’s $4.88 billion market capitalization already embeds a 2.7x growth of captured revenue at a mature fee multiple — essentially the volume level at which, post-inflation-cut, net issuance flips negative. Current data (capture rising to 39.2%, a funded and outbound-free buyback wallet, a passed 36% mint cut) is consistent with that path but does not exceed it. We find no evidence of a valuation gap on the metrics we can re-run; we find a fairly priced bet on execution. Position sizing should reflect execution risk, and the falsifiers below — not conviction — should drive revisions.

Chapter 6

Risks, Counterarguments, and Invalidation Criteria

Counterarguments to the deflationary story

1.Buybacks are not burns

The 2.25 million NEAR in the buyback multisig is custodied, not destroyed. Nothing in the protocol forces destruction; the wallet could later stake, sell, or fund operations, converting the sink into a shadow treasury. The dashboard’s own materials acknowledge the distinction between tokens bought and tokens permanently removed. Mitigation is structural: falsifier F4 watches wallet outflows continuously, and any material distribution changes the model’s arithmetic same-day.

2.Take-rate fragility

The 6.28 basis-point effective take is an average across three mechanisms, and intent-based trading is a contested category: ERC-7683-style standards, exchange-owned aggregators, and solver fee wars can all compress it. A halving of the take rate doubles every V* estimate in Chapter 4. Capture has been rising (19.5% lifetime to 28–39% recent), but two months of improvement is a trend, not a law.

3.Volume quality and concentration

Intents volume includes aggregator-routed and possibly incentive-influenced flow, and the owned front-end accounted for roughly a quarter of Q3 volume by third-party accounting — efficient for capture, fragile for resilience. The L1 contraction (Chapter 3) means the “broad network usage” story has already failed once; the surviving thesis is narrower.

4.Regulatory surface

Tokenized US equities and ETFs on near.com, confidential settlement (including $2.6 billion-plus of ZEC), and a staking ETF sit close to policy lines; the platform’s own SHIELD controls rejected more than $50 million of Bitget-hack-linked transfers in late September, which demonstrates controls and exposure in equal measure (cited, not re-runnable).

5.Macro beta

97% annualized volatility and a −30% month show the asset trades with crypto risk appetite; nothing in this model hedges a sector-wide multiple compression. ETF flows are the one structural demand item that is cited, not re-runnable: the Bitwise NRR (launched 29 September 2026, staking 100% of holdings) and Grayscale’s pending conversion create a new holder channel whose flows must be tracked manually.

Symmetrically, the thesis strengthens if: capture holds above 40% of gross for a quarter; the V* coverage ratio (current volume over V*) rises through 0.5 on a sustained basis; the staking ratio holds above 40% through the first year of the inflation cut; and confidential TVL re-accelerates after its October consolidation. None of these require narrative — they are one-line API checks, which is the point of the evidence standard.

Conclusion

The re-runnable evidence describes a project in mid-transition with the pivot roughly half-paid-for. Demand compounds: $37.3 billion settled all-time, 88% of it in the last twelve months, at 3.3 times the year-ago 90-day pace. Capture scales: net revenue up from $27.6 thousand to $2.50 million per month in fourteen months, with the monthly capture rate at 39.2% and the buyback wallet accumulating 2.25 million NEAR with zero observed outflows. Supply tightens on a committed schedule: a passed 36% reduction in maximum inflation, which cuts the deflation crossover to 2.6 times current volume. Against that, the layer-1’s own usage has contracted 83% year-over-year, DeFi TVL is shrinking, the fee base is one product wide, and price shows no daily tether to the fundamental series.

The valuation absorbs the improvement. At 163 times captured revenue — or 68.3 times gross fees — the market capitalization already pays for bull-case volume at a mature multiple; the base case at a mature multiple prices NEAR materially below spot. That is what “priced for delivery” means operationally: the investor’s edge cannot be the observation that NEAR has a revenue engine, because the market has priced the engine; the edge, if any, is in monitoring whether delivery beats or misses the embedded path — weekly, from public endpoints, using the falsifier dashboard above and the one-command reproduction script in Appendix B. Judged on the evidence and not the conviction: hold-with-verification, add only on outperformance, exit on the falsifiers.

A.4 On-chain activity via BigQuery (no key required)

The daily activity series used in this report was pulled from NearBlocks’ free API. The same series — and any longer history — is re-runnable from Google’s public dataset with any free Google account (BigQuery Sandbox; querying bigquery-public-data does not require billing):

BigQuery SQL — re-run in the BigQuery console (Sandbox, free)

-- Daily transactions and active accounts, NEAR mainnet
-- Dataset: bigquery-public-data.crypto_near (free; no API key)
SELECT DATE(block_timestamp) AS date,
       COUNT(*)              AS txns,
       COUNT(DISTINCT signer_account_id) AS active_accounts
FROM `bigquery-public-data.crypto_near.transactions`
WHERE DATE(block_timestamp) BETWEEN '2025-11-01' AND '2026-11-10'
GROUP BY date ORDER BY date;

-- Buyback wallet flow audit (all history)
SELECT DATE(block_timestamp) AS date,
       predecessor_account_id AS from_acct,
       receiver_account_id    AS to_acct,
       COUNT(*) AS txns
FROM `bigquery-public-data.crypto_near.transactions`
WHERE receiver_account_id = 'buybacks.multisignature.near'
   OR predecessor_account_id = 'buybacks.multisignature.near'
GROUP BY date, from_acct, to_acct ORDER BY date;

B.2 Formulas

Model formulas (used for every derived figure in this report)

P/S (gross)        = MarketCap / (Fees_30d * 365/30)
Effective take tau = NetRevenue_month / Volume_month         (bps = tau * 10^4)
Mint_per_day       = i * S / 365                             (NEAR)
V* (USD/day)       = (i * S / 365 * P) / tau                 [deflation threshold]
Offset ratio       = NetRevenue_NEAR_month / Mint_NEAR_month
Staking yield      = i * 0.90 / staking_ratio                (90% staker share)
Buyback yield      = NetRevenue_month * 12 / MarketCap
Scenario revenue   = Volume_day * 365 * tau                  (annualized net revenue)
Lead-lag           = Pearson r( price log-returns_t , volume log-growth_{t+lag} ),
                     lags -14..+14 days
YoY volume         = trailing365_volume / prior365_volume    (7.5x at retrieval)

B.3 Reference code

The complete reproduction script ships with this report as NEAR_thesis_reproduce.py (single file; requires only requests and matplotlib; runtime about one minute; no API keys). It re-fetches every endpoint in Appendix A, recomputes every derived metric in B.2, and regenerates all nine figures. The core of the V* and multiple models, condensed:

Python — V* and fee-multiple models (condensed from NEAR_thesis_reproduce.py)

import requests, json
near = requests.get("https://api.coinpaprika.com/v1/tickers/near-near-protocol").json()
P = near["quotes"]["USD"]["price"]; mcap = near["quotes"]["USD"]["market_cap"]
S = near["total_supply"]
vol = requests.get("https://api.llama.fi/summary/dexs/near-intents"
                   "?dataType=dailyVolume").json()
fees= requests.get("https://api.llama.fi/summary/fees/near-intents"
                   "?dataType=dailyFees").json()
# net revenue month: parse revenue.near.org embedded series (see full script)
net_rev_oct, vol_oct = 2_502_470, 3.99e9           # 2026-11-11 readings
tau = net_rev_oct / vol_oct                        # effective take (bps = tau*1e4)
for i in (0.025, 0.016):                           # current vs HSP-029 target
    mint_day = i * S / 365                         # NEAR minted per day
    v_star   = mint_day * P / tau                  # USD/day volume to offset mint
    print(f"i={i:.1%}: mint {mint_day:,.0f} NEAR/d, V* ${v_star/1e6:,.0f}M/d")
ps_gross = mcap / (fees["total30d"] / 30 * 365)    # P/S on gross fees
ps_net   = mcap / (net_rev_oct * 12)               # P/S on captured revenue
print(f"P/S gross {ps_gross:.0f}x | P/S net {ps_net:.0f}x")

Method notes. The effective take uses October 2026 as the cleanest full month (post-capture-improvement); using the trailing-30d window instead yields 6.4 basis points and shifts V* by under 2%. The staker share of issuance (90%) follows the HSP-029 documentation and reconciles with independent yield estimates; the appendix script computes both 90% and 100% variants. NearBlocks’ anonymous pagination window covers the latest 250 wallet transactions; the full 3,339-transaction history is auditable via the BigQuery SQL in Appendix A.4. All charts in this report are regenerable from the same script.
